summary: This best current practice gives guidelines for authors and reviewers of specifications that contain YANG data models, including IANA-maintained modules. It aims to improve interoperability and usability of NETCONF and RESTCONF. It obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126.

eli5.summary: This is a style guide for writing the blueprints that describe network devices. Following it keeps them consistent and easy to review.

subtitle: The style and review rulebook for any RFC or draft that contains a YANG data model, now with rules for IANA-maintained modules.

tldr.problem: YANG leaves many constructs optional and allows things that servers are not required to support, so modules written without shared rules are hard to read, review and implement interoperably.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets documentation rules (required sections, code markers, security and IANA text, examples), YANG usage rules (naming, XPath, data types, lifecycle, operational state) and a review checklist, plus a template for IANA-maintained modules.
tldr.outcome: It is BCP 216, obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126 with guidance on writing IANA Considerations for IANA-maintained YANG modules.

facts.value: ietf- for IETF, iana- for IANA-maintained

today: RFC 9907 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 216). It obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 9907 defines guidelines for documents that contain YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950) and YANG 1.0 (RFC 6020) data models, including IANA-maintained YANG modules. YANG describes the data structures, protocol operations and notification content of a NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040) server, and it can also define abstract data structures (RFC 8791).

Many YANG constructs, such as the description statement, are optional, and YANG allows things like infinite-length identifiers or top-level mandatory nodes that a compliant server need not support. The guidelines ask for a higher level of compliance, and only constructs that all servers are required to support may be used in IETF YANG modules.

The RFC is not a YANG tutorial. Authors and reviewers can use it independent of the IETF Stream, or even in other organizations. It obsoletes RFC 8407, and its Section 4.30.3 updates RFC 8126. Compared with RFC 8407 it adds, among other things, guidelines for IANA-maintained YANG modules, a section on classifying modules, a section on modeling abstract data structures, a template for IANA registrations and guidance on the use of the terms YANG module and YANG data model.
sections.eli5: YANG is a language for describing how to set up network gear. This guide is the list of manners for writing in that language, so everyone's descriptions are clear and nothing is left half-specified.

sections.title: Terminology: Data Model versus Module
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms used throughout. An IETF module is a YANG module published by the IETF that is not maintained by IANA. An IANA-maintained YANG module has an IANA registry associated with it, such as iana-tunnel-type. Once it is initialized, new values are not added to the module directly but to the companion registry. A module is published when it is a stable release, for example in an RFC, and unpublished when it is an unstable one, for example in an Internet-Draft.

A YANG data model describes how data is represented and accessed, and it can consist of one YANG module or several. A YANG module is a self-contained block of definitions, typically one .yang file. The term YANG model should be avoided in favor of YANG data model, and YANG data module has no meaning and must be avoided.

Use YANG data model in the title, abstract and the body where the overall design is described, even if it is a single module. Use YANG module when a specific *.yang file is referenced or when discussing augmentation or deviation.
sections.eli5: A data model is the whole story about how some data is organized. A module is one file of that story. Use the right word for the right thing so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Required Document Structure
sections.content:
A document with a YANG module MUST have narrative sections and a Definitions section, and it MUST add YANG-specific content to its Security Considerations, IANA Considerations and References sections.

  • Copyright. The module description MUST reference the latest approved IETF Trust Copyright statement.
  • Code components. Each normative module is a code component marked with <CODE BEGINS> and <CODE ENDS>. The begin tag MUST be followed by a file name, and the name form with the revision date SHOULD be used. Example modules are not code components and are named like example-toaster.
  • Narrative. An overview section MUST describe scope and the relationship to other standards. Modules should be written in YANG 1.1, and YANG 1.0 may be used if no YANG 1.1 features are needed. Authors SHOULD also mention the module classification: a service model, network model or device model.
  • Tree diagrams. They SHOULD be included, and ones longer than one page SHOULD go in an appendix.
  • Examples. Documents SHOULD include usage examples in XML or JSON, validated with tools such as pyang, yanglint or yangson, using values reserved for documentation, such as Enterprise Number 32473.
  • References. Every import or include of a module from another document needs a matching normative reference.

Example modules and fragments MUST NOT contain normative text, including RFC 2119 key words. In a normative module, every YANG statement is normative.
sections.eli5: Every document with a blueprint must come with the same parts: an explanation, the blueprint itself with clear start and end markers, and examples that have been checked, so a reader can find and test everything.

sections.title: YANG Usage Guidelines
sections.content:
Section 4 adds rules on top of the YANG specification. Only guidelines that clarify or restrict the minimum conformance requirements are included. Modules in IETF Standards Track documents MUST comply with all syntactic and semantic requirements of YANG 1.1.

Names. All normative IETF module names MUST start with ietf- and all IANA-maintained module names with iana-. Published module names must be unique and MUST NOT be reused, even if the RFC becomes Historic. Identifiers in published modules MUST be 1 to 64 characters long. They should use only lowercase letters, numbers and dashes, and list identifiers should be singular with a plural container name. Identifiers should not carry modeling semantics: calling a node config or state does not change whether it is configuration or state.

XPath. The position, last, id, namespace-uri, name and lang functions SHOULD NOT be used, and derived-from-or-self should be used for identityref values. The preceding and following axes SHOULD NOT be used. The int64 and uint64 types SHOULD NOT be used in numeric or boolean expressions, because XPath numbers only have 53 bits of precision.

Lifecycle and headers. The organization, contact and description statements MUST be present, and a revision statement with a reference MUST exist for each published version. Module names and namespace URIs MUST NOT change once published. The status SHOULD NOT go straight from current to obsolete, and an object SHOULD stay available for at least one year after its publication date with the deprecated status. Top-level data definitions MUST NOT be mandatory.

Data types and constructs. Use the most appropriate built-in type, order union members from most to least restrictive, and use identityref instead of an enumeration when distributed extensibility is needed. The when statement silently deletes data when its condition becomes false, whereas must causes a validation error. Use the structure extension from RFC 8791 rather than yang-data for abstract data structures.
sections.eli5: These are the small rules of good writing: give things clear and unique names, do not use tricky tools that behave differently on different machines, and never change a published name, because other people already rely on it.

sections.title: Operational State and NMDA
sections.content:
Operational state used to mean only config false data, which was not part of any datastore. Under the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342) it is conceptually in the operational state datastore, which also holds the operational values of configuration data. There is no longer a need to duplicate structures into separate configuration and state sections.

If possible, operational state SHOULD be combined with its configuration data. That avoids duplicate keys and ancestor nodes, avoids race conditions when retrieving dynamic entries, and lets both be fetched together. The same data type SHOULD represent the configured and operational value of a leaf. When they differ, as with admin-status and oper-status, separate objects MAY be used.

YANG modules SHOULD be designed assuming servers support the operational state datastore, and designers SHOULD describe and justify any NMDA exceptions in the module's description statements. If a document has major NMDA exceptions or a temporary non-NMDA module, its Introduction SHOULD say so and why.
sections.eli5: A thermostat has a setting you chose and a temperature the room actually has. This part says to keep both in the same place on the blueprint when you can, so they are easy to compare.

sections.title: Security Considerations Template
sections.content:
Each specification that defines modules MUST contain a Security Considerations section modeled after the latest approved template, which is kept on an IETF wiki page and reproduced in Section 3.7.1. Documents that exclusively define modules following RFC 8791, or that define YANG extensions such as RFC 7952, are not required to use it.

The template states that the data model is designed to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, which have to use a secure transport layer and mutual authentication. It points to the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) for restricting access. Then it has sections to be kept or dropped:

  • Writable data nodes (config true) that could be especially disruptive MUST be listed by name with the risks explained.
  • Readable data nodes that hold sensitive information or raise privacy concerns MUST be listed by name with the reasons.
  • RPC or action operations that are potentially harmful MUST be listed with the reasons.
  • A reminder when groupings from other modules are reused, and a short text for modules that define only identities, types and groupings.

The RFC's own Security Considerations section says the document defines guidelines only and introduces no new or increased security risks.
sections.eli5: Every blueprint must come with a warning label: which settings could cause damage if a stranger changed them, and which readings could reveal private things. It is a fill-in-the-blanks safety sheet.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and IANA-Maintained Modules
sections.content:
Each normative module MUST be registered in both the IETF XML Registry (the ns registry) and the YANG Module Names registry. The request should say whether the module is IANA-maintained. The RFC provides templates for registering new modules and for revising existing ones. RFC 9907 itself registers the ietf-template and iana-template namespaces and modules, both marked as not maintained by IANA, and updates the YANG Module Names reference from RFC 8407 to itself.

The larger new part is the guidance for IANA-maintained YANG modules. When a protocol has an IANA registry, the RFC RECOMMENDS an IANA-maintained module that echoes the registry, since a copy of the values inside an IETF module could drift from the registry as values are assigned or deprecated. A module can use identityref or enumeration, and the reason for the choice MUST be documented.

The defining RFC may supply the initial module or only a script that generates it. It MUST say it documents only the initial version and that the authoritative version comes from IANA, and the module MUST carry a note naming the RFC that registered it. Its IANA Considerations MUST ask IANA to add notes to the module page and to the registry, and MUST describe how to add a new identity or enum when the registry changes, including how to turn registry names into legal identifiers, for example one that begins with a digit.
sections.eli5: When a master list is kept by a librarian, the blueprint copy of that list must be kept by the librarian too, not by the authors. This section tells the librarian exactly how to update the copy each time the master list changes.

sections.title: Module Review Checklist
sections.content:
Appendix A adapts the checklist from RFC 4181 for reviewers. The checklist goes through the boilerplate and abstract, the copyright notice, the Security Considerations section (modeled on the template unless an exception applies), the IANA Considerations section, the references and the license.

It requires an IANA Considerations section that registers each module's namespace in the XML Namespace Registry and its name, prefix, namespace and RFC number in the YANG Module Registry. It also checks that references are split between normative and informative, that all YANG modules containing imported items are cited as normative references, and that each YANG module carries the Revised BSD License.

For technical content, a YANG module compiler is recommended for syntax errors, but the checklist stresses that syntax is only part of the job. The reviewer should read the document from an implementor's point of view and check that description statements are clear and unambiguous enough for interoperable implementations. Appendices B and C supply module templates for IETF and IANA-maintained modules.
sections.eli5: Reviewers get a checklist, like a teacher checking homework: are all the parts present, are the sources listed, is the warning label filled in, and would a stranger be able to follow the instructions?

    }
